title: Stone Points From Arabia May Have Carried Poison
paragraphs: Around 125,000 years ago, the Empty Quarter of Saudi Arabia held a freshwater lake, and a new paper in the journal Science suggests that the people who gathered on its shore were skilled hunters. Researchers from Griffith University, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology and the Saudi Heritage Commission examined a site called 'Uruq Aljelibah, where they recovered more than 5,000 stone artefacts alongside fossils of hippos, buffalo, camels, gazelles and oryx.

Microscopic analysis found animal tissue near the tips of some stone points and plant resin and fibres at their bases, which indicates that the points were attached to shafts. Several also showed impact damage consistent with hunting large animals. "This suggests people were manufacturing composite weapons made from multiple materials," said lead researcher Christopher Clarkson. The distribution of the tools closely matched clusters of animal bones, so the shore may have been a focal point for hunting and processing game.

The most striking claim is also the most cautious one. Chemical markers linked to Acokanthera schimperi, a tree that contains toxic compounds, were found on several points, and the team says this raises the possibility of poisoned weapons. Poison use is inferred rather than confirmed, and the press release does not give exact counts, so the finding should be treated as an interesting hypothesis.

questions.q: What did the microscopic analysis suggest about the stone points?
questions.a: That they were fixed to shafts with resin and fibres.

questions.q: What evidence connects the site to hunting?
questions.a: Impact damage on points, and tools matching clusters of animal bones.

questions.q: Why should the poison claim be treated with care?
questions.a: Poison use is inferred, not confirmed, and no exact counts were given.
